Statement

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), the C*-algebra completion interface of [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]], and the finite-matrix positive square-root interface of [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]]. Let $\{\rho_\Lambda\}$ be a consistent family of finite local density matrices as in [[lem-qsm-consistent-local-states]], and let $\omega$ be its extended algebraic state on the unital quasi-local algebra $\mathcal A$. Then there are a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H_\omega$, a unital $*$-representation $\pi_\omega:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\omega)$, and a unit vector $\Omega_\omega$ cyclic for $\pi_\omega$ such that

$$\omega(A)=\langle \pi_\omega(A)\Omega_\omega,\Omega_\omega\rangle\qquad(A\in\mathcal A),$$

using the linear-first inner-product convention. Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\omega)$ is the space of bounded linear operators with its operator norm, a $*$-representation is a complex-linear map preserving products, adjoints and the identity, and cyclic means that $\{\pi_\omega(A)\Omega_\omega:A\in\mathcal A\}$ is norm dense in $\mathcal H_\omega$. The theorem asserts existence of a cyclic representation, not uniqueness up to unitary equivalence.

external_items.interface:
Definition

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $\mathcal B(H)$ denote
its bounded linear operators. Applying AC to a family indexed by the natural numbers
supplies Countable Choice, the hypothesis of
[[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]], which provides adjoints on $\mathcal B(H)$.
A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a
unital $*$-subalgebra $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ that is closed in the
weak operator topology (WOT). Here unital means $I_H\in\mathcal A$; the zero
Hilbert space is allowed, with $I_H=0$ and sole unital algebra $\{0\}$. This is
the only use of AC in this definition.

For any set $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, its **commutant** and
**double commutant** are
$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):TS=ST\text{ for every }S\in\mathcal S\},\qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$
Commutants are taken inside $\mathcal B(H)$. The **von Neumann algebra
generated by $\mathcal S$** is
$$W^*(\mathcal S):=\overline{\operatorname{Alg}^*(\mathcal S\cup\{I_H\})}^{\,\mathrm{WOT}},$$
the WOT closure in $\mathcal B(H)$ of the unital $*$-algebra generated by
$\mathcal S$. No bicommutant theorem is part of these definitions.

Two elementary properties will be used. For fixed $S\in\mathcal B(H)$,
$$\langle TS\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle T(S\xi),\eta\rangle,\qquad \langle ST\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle T\xi,S^*\eta\rangle$$
are WOT-continuous matrix coefficients as functions of $T$. Thus each equation
$TS=ST$ defines a WOT-closed set, and so $\mathcal S'$ is WOT-closed. If
$\mathcal S$ is self-adjoint, then $\mathcal S'$ is a unital $*$-subalgebra:
products preserve commutation with every $S$, and taking adjoints of $TS=ST$
gives $ST^*=T^*S$. These facts do not identify $W^*(\mathcal S)$ with
$\mathcal S''$.

Definition

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Then $M''=M$, and $M$ is also closed in the strong operator topology. Consequently the concrete von Neumann algebras of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]] are exactly the unital $*$-subalgebras that are closed in either of these topologies. For an arbitrary set $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ one has $W^*(\mathcal S)''=W^*(\mathcal S)$.

Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Definition

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Statement

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root convention that its inner product is linear in the first argument, and let $\rho$ be a density operator on $H$ ([[def-qc-density-operator]]). If $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$ are its eigenvalues counted with multiplicity, define its **von Neumann entropy** by

$$S(\rho):=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho\ln\rho):=-\sum_{j:\lambda_j>0}\lambda_j\ln\lambda_j.$$

The trace is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]), and the spectral definition makes the expression independent of the eigenbasis. The term for a zero eigenvalue is defined to be $0\ln0:=0$. The default unit is nats, using the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]); the entropy in bits is $S_2(\rho):=S(\rho)/\ln2$.

Definition

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $A,B:H\to H$ be non-negative operators. For such an operator $A$, set $\operatorname{supp}(A):=(\ker A)^\perp$, where $\ker A$ is the kernel of a linear map ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]); this extends the density-operator support convention in [[def-qc-density-operator]]. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, define

$$D(A\|B):=\operatorname{tr}(A\ln A)-\operatorname{tr}(A\ln B).$$

Here $\ln A$ is defined spectrally on the positive eigenspaces of $A$ with $0\ln0:=0$, and $\ln B$ in the cross term is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}(B)$; the support condition ensures that $A$ vanishes on $\ker B$, so the omitted kernel contributes zero. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\nsubseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, set $D(A\|B):=+\infty$. In particular, $D(0\|B)=0$. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional **quantum relative entropy**. The logarithms are natural, so the value is in nats; the base-two value is $D_2(A\|B):=D(A\|B)/\ln2$.

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

Let $H=H^*$ act on a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension $d\geq1$, $\beta>0$, $k_B>0$, $T=(k_B\beta)^{-1}$, and $Z=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})$. Put $\sigma=e^{-\beta H}/Z$, $F_\beta=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$, and $S(\rho)=-k_B\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$, with $0\log0=0$. Then every density matrix $\rho$, including rank-deficient matrices, satisfies
$
\operatorname{Tr}(\rho H)-TS(\rho)\geq F_\beta,
$
with equality if and only if $\rho=\sigma$. Moreover $S(\sigma)=k_B(\log Z+\beta\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma H))$, so $F_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma H)-TS(\sigma)$. This is finite-dimensional mathematical optimization; actual preparation is a separate postulate.

Definition

Use the lattice $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, $d\ge1$, the finite spin dimension $q\ge1$, the local matrix algebras $\mathcal A_\Lambda$, and the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty$ of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]]. For finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$, write $\operatorname{diam}_\infty Z=\max_{x,y\in Z}d_\infty(x,y)$; for finite nonempty $X,Y\subset\Gamma$, write $\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,Y)=\min_{x\in X,y\in Y}d_\infty(x,y)$.

A **uniformly bounded finite-range interaction** is a family $\Phi(Z)\in\mathcal A_Z$, indexed by finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$, such that $\Phi(Z)^*=\Phi(Z)$ and there are an integer $M\ge1$, a finite $R\ge0$, and $\kappa<\infty$ satisfying

$$\Phi(Z)=0\quad\text{if }|Z|>M\text{ or }\operatorname{diam}_\infty Z>R,\qquad\kappa:=\sup_{x\in\Gamma}\sum_{Z\ni x}\|\Phi(Z)\|<\infty.$$

The norm in this sum is the operator norm in the local matrix algebra $\mathcal A_Z$. If a model lists several terms with the same support, first add them in that local algebra; the resulting single operator is $\Phi(Z)$, and $\kappa$ uses its norm. Thus no multiplicity is implicit.

For a finite region $\Lambda\subset\Gamma$, define the **free-boundary finite-volume Hamiltonian** by summing only terms whose complete support lies inside $\Lambda$; terms meeting $\Lambda$ but extending outside it are omitted:

$$H_\Lambda:=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi(Z)\in\mathcal A_\Lambda.$$

It is a finite sum of self-adjoint matrices. For a fixed scale $\hbar>0$ and any finite $\Omega\supseteq\Lambda$, embed $H_\Lambda$ in $\mathcal A_\Omega$ by the canonical factor inclusion and define

$$\alpha_t^\Lambda(A):=e^{itH_\Lambda/\hbar}Ae^{-itH_\Lambda/\hbar}\qquad(A\in\mathcal A_\Omega,\ t\in\mathbb R).$$

These actions are compatible as $\Omega$ increases, because the extra tensor factors carry the identity. On $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ this is the ordinary finite matrix Heisenberg dynamics.

In physical SI bookkeeping, when $\Phi(Z)$ is interpreted as an energy, $\Phi(Z)$, $\kappa$, and $H_\Lambda$ have units J, $t$ has units s, and $\hbar$ is the adopted reduced Planck constant with units J s. The mathematics below uses only $\hbar>0$ and asserts no measured parameter value.

Let $\mu>0$, let $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$ be finite, let $X\subseteq\Lambda$ be finite and nonempty, and let $Y\subset\mathbb Z^d$ be any finite nonempty set. Take $A\in\mathcal A_X$ and $B\in\mathcal A_Y$, with both embedded in the common finite algebra $\mathcal A_{\Lambda\cup Y}$. Then for every $t\in\mathbb R$,

$$\bigl\|[\alpha_t^\Lambda(A),B]\bigr\|\le 2\|A\|\,\|B\|\,|X|\exp\!\left(\frac{2\kappa M e^{\mu R}}{\hbar}|t|-\mu\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,Y)\right).$$

Here the finite-volume dynamics is extended by the identity on sites outside $\Lambda$, as in [[def-qsm-bounded-finite-range-interaction]]. The parameter $\mu$ is measured per lattice step in the dimensionless max-coordinate metric. The bound is uniform over finite volumes containing $X$; it is an operator-norm estimate for the stipulated spin model, not a relativistic light cone.

Definition

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$, the countable site set $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^d$ of [[lem-qsm-integer-lattice-countable]], and one finite spin dimension $q\ge1$, where $q$ is a positive integer (so $q\in\mathbb N$ and $1\le q$, by [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-nat-order]]). For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define $|n|=n$ if $0\le n$ and $|n|=-n$ if $n<0$, using the integer order and additive inverse of [[def-int-order]] and [[def-int-operations]]. Totality and compatibility of the integer order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]) give $0\le|n|$ and $-|n|\le n\le|n|$. Adding these bounds for $m,n\in\mathbb Z$ gives $|m+n|\le|m|+|n|$. Equip $\Gamma$ with the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_{1\le r\le d}|x_r-y_r|$; the maximum exists because the coordinate set is finite and nonempty, symmetry and separation hold coordinatewise, and the absolute-value triangle inequality gives $|x_r-z_r|\le|x_r-y_r|+|y_r-z_r|$ for every coordinate, hence the triangle inequality for $d_\infty$. A **finite region** is a finite subset $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$; its cardinality is $|\Lambda|$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]).

For a finite region $\Lambda$, let $S_\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,q\}^{\Lambda}$ be the set of spin configurations on $\Lambda$. Induction on $|\Lambda|$ gives $|S_\Lambda|=q^{|\Lambda|}$: the empty region has one configuration, and for $x\in\Lambda$ the restriction map $s\mapsto(s|_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}},s(x))$ is a bijection $S_\Lambda\to S_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}}\times\{1,\ldots,q\}$, so adjoining one site multiplies the number of configurations by $q$, according to the recursion defining natural-number powers in [[def-nat-power]]. Let $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ be the vector space of functions $f:S_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}f(s)\overline{g(s)}$. For each $s\in S_\Lambda$, let $e_s$ be the indicator function of $\{s\}$; these vectors form an orthonormal basis. For $\Lambda=\varnothing$, $S_\Lambda$ is a singleton and $\mathcal H_\Lambda\cong\mathbb C$. The **local spin matrix algebra** is

$$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space; they are bounded. The algebra has composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity $I_\Lambda$, and induced operator norm

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

The **finite local trace** is $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(T):=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}\langle T e_s,e_s\rangle$ in the displayed configuration basis $(e_s)$. This is the usual finite-matrix trace; basis independence and its cyclic/unitary identities are supplied by [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]].

If $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, restriction of configurations gives the canonical factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$, with sites ordered lexicographically. The **factor inclusion** is the unital $*$-homomorphism $\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}:\mathcal A_\Lambda\to\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}$ given by $T\mapsto T\otimes I_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$. A **localization region** for $T$ is any finite $\Lambda$ for which $T\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ under these inclusions; a localization region need not be minimal.

The ordinary operator norm makes each local matrix algebra a nonzero unital complete C*-algebra, and every positive normalized complex-linear functional is uniquely a trace pairing with a density matrix, by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]]. This includes the empty region, whose Hilbert space is $\mathbb C$. This definition does not posit an infinite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert space.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $k$ be a field with

$$R_Q|a\rangle=\omega_Q^a|a\rangle,\qquad M_Q|a\rangle=|a-1\!\pmod Q\rangle.$$

$$R_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad M_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix};\qquad R_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&e^{2\pi i/3}&0\\0&0&e^{4\pi i/3}\end{pmatrix},\quad M_3=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

Let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space of finite dimension $d\ge1$, $H=H^*$ with energy unit J, $\hbar>0$ with unit J s, $\beta>0$ with unit J$^{-1}$, and let $\sigma=Z_\beta^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$ be the stationary Gibbs density from [[thm-qsm-dt-finite-unitary]]. Let $A=A^*$ and $B=B^*$ be matrices, let $T>0$ be finite in s, let $h:[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let $\epsilon\in\mathbb R$ be dimensionless; $h(t)B$ has unit J. Put $U_0(t)=e^{-itH/\hbar}$ for time $t$ in s, $\alpha_t(A)=U_0(t)^*AU_0(t)$, and $B_t=\alpha_t(B)$. Let $W_\epsilon$ solve
$$W_\epsilon'(t)=\frac{i\epsilon h(t)}{\hbar}B_tW_\epsilon(t),\qquad W_\epsilon(0)=I,$$
and set $U_\epsilon(t)=U_0(t)W_\epsilon(t)$ and $\rho_I(t)=W_\epsilon(t)\sigma W_\epsilon(t)^*$. Then $U_\epsilon$ solves $i\hbar U_\epsilon'(t)=(H-\epsilon h(t)B)U_\epsilon(t)$, $U_\epsilon(0)=I$, and $\rho_\epsilon(t):=U_\epsilon(t)\sigma U_\epsilon(t)^*$ satisfies $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\epsilon(t)A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_I(t)\alpha_t(A))$. Define
$$R_{AB}(u)=\frac{i}{\hbar}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\sigma[\alpha_u(A),B]\right),\qquad C_T=\frac{2}{\hbar}\int_0^T|h(s)|\,\|B\|\,ds.$$
Then $W_\epsilon(t)$ is unitary and, for $0\le t\le T$,
$$\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_I(t)\alpha_t(A))=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma\alpha_t(A))+\epsilon\int_0^t h(s)R_{AB}(t-s)\,ds+r_\epsilon(t),\qquad |r_\epsilon(t)|\le\|A\|\frac{(|\epsilon|C_T)^2e^{|\epsilon|C_T}}2.$$
The initial Gibbs matrix is fixed as $\epsilon$ varies. The result is an exact finite-time first variation with a controlled remainder, not a static derivative of a re-prepared Gibbs family. $C_T$ and $\epsilon$ are dimensionless, and $R_{AB}$ has units $[A][B]/(\mathrm J\,\mathrm s)$.

Let $I$ and $\mathcal F_\pm(\ell^2(I))$ be as in
[[def-qsm-identical-particle-fock-sectors]]. Define
$$
\Omega_B:=\{m:I\to\mathbb N_0:m\text{ has finite support}\},\qquad \Omega_F:=\{m:I\to\{0,1\}:m\text{ has finite support}\}.
$$
For either statistics choice, write $|m|=\sum_jm_j$. If $m\in\Omega_B$, choose the elementary tensor $x_m$ containing $m_j$ copies of each mode $j$ in the fixed order and set
$$
|m\rangle_B:=\sqrt{\frac{|m|!}{\prod_jm_j!}}\,P_+^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
If $m\in\Omega_F$, list its occupied modes increasingly in the fixed enumeration, let $x_m$ be their elementary tensor and set
$$
|m\rangle_F:=\sqrt{|m|!}\,P_-^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
For $|m|=0$, both vectors are the vacuum. These vectors form orthonormal bases and define unitary identifications $\mathcal F_+(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_B)$ and $\mathcal F_-(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_F)$.

On the finite-support span $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ of the bosonic basis, define
$$
a_j|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j}|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,\qquad a_j^\dagger|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j+1}|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,
$$
where the annihilation term is zero when $m_j=0$. Their maximal closed extensions have domains
$$
D(a_j)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}m_j|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(a_j^\dagger)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}(m_j+1)|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},
$$
and $a_j^\dagger=a_j^*$. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, they satisfy
$[a_i,a_j^\dagger]=\delta_{ij}I$, $[a_i,a_j]=0$, and $[a_i^\dagger,a_j^\dagger]=0$.

On the fermionic basis define
$$
c_j|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}m_j|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_F,\qquad c_j^\dagger|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}(1-m_j)|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_F.
$$
These operators are bounded on the full fermionic Fock space and satisfy
$\{c_i,c_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}I$ and $\{c_i,c_j\}=\{c_i^\dagger,c_j^\dagger\}=0$. These are mathematical sector relations; they do not select a physical species or imply a spin-statistics theorem.

Assume [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $I$ be finite or countably infinite with a specified enumeration, let $m\in\Omega_\pm$ be the occupation configurations of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]], and let $\epsilon_j\in\mathbb R$ be finite mode energies. For each finite-support configuration put
$$
E(m):=\sum_j\epsilon_jm_j,\qquad N(m):=|m|=\sum_jm_j.
$$
These are finite sums. On $\ell^2(\Omega_\pm)$, define the real diagonal multipliers
$$
D(H)=\left\{c:\sum_mE(m)^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Hc)_m=E(m)c_m,
$$
$$
D(N)=\left\{c:\sum_m|m|^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Nc)_m=|m|c_m,
$$
and, for $\mu\in\mathbb R$,
$$
D(K_\mu)=\left\{c:\sum_m|E(m)-\mu|m||^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (K_\mu c)_m=(E(m)-\mu|m|)c_m.
$$
Each is self-adjoint on its displayed domain. No equality between $D(K_\mu)$ and $D(H)\cap D(N)$ is asserted.

For $\beta>0$, set $q_j=e^{-\beta(\epsilon_j-\mu)}$. In the bosonic case assume
$$
0<q_j<1,\qquad q_*:=\sup_jq_j<1,\qquad \sum_jq_j<\infty;
$$
Here $q_*=0$ by convention when $I$ is empty; for nonempty $I$ the displayed supremum is unchanged. In the fermionic case assume $q_j>0$, $\sum_jq_j<\infty$, and only finitely many gaps $\epsilon_j-\mu$ are negative. Define the positive diagonal multiplier $G_{\beta,\mu}$ by $G_{\beta,\mu}|m\rangle=e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}|m\rangle$. Then $G_{\beta,\mu}$ is trace class, with
$$
\Xi_B=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty,\qquad \Xi_F=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1+q_j)<\infty.
$$
Thus $\rho_{\beta,\mu}=\Xi^{-1}G_{\beta,\mu}$ is a positive trace-class operator of trace one. Its finite-mode marginals are independent: bosonic occupation $n_j\in\mathbb N_0$ has law $(1-q_j)q_j^{n_j}$, and fermionic occupation $n_j\in\{0,1\}$ has probabilities $(1+q_j)^{-1}$ and $q_j(1+q_j)^{-1}$. In particular
$$
\mathbb E_BN_j=\frac{q_j}{1-q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_B(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1-q_j)^2},\qquad \mathbb E_FN_j=\frac{q_j}{1+q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_F(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1+q_j)^2}.
$$
The total number has finite mean and variance under the stated mode conditions. The trace hypotheses alone do not imply finite energy moments or differentiability in $\beta,\mu$.

For an additional compact-parameter envelope, the corresponding response identities hold. For fixed $\mu$, let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be a nonempty open interval. If for every compact $B\subset J$ a summable $(a_m)$ satisfies $(1+|E(m)-\mu|m||^2)e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}\le a_m$ for all $m$ and $\beta\in B$, then throughout $J$, $-\partial_\beta\log\Xi=\mathbb E(K_\mu)$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log\Xi=\operatorname{Var}(K_\mu)$. If $(\beta,\mu)$ varies over an open set and a summable compact-parameter envelope dominates $e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}(1+|E(m)|^2+|m|^2)$, then at fixed $\beta$, $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(N)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(N)$ and $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(E)=\beta\operatorname{Cov}(E,N)$. These stronger moment envelopes are additional hypotheses, not consequences of trace-class normalization.

For a finite mode set $J$, the canonical fixed-number coefficients are defined by
$$
\prod_{j\in J}(1-ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})^{-1}=\sum_{N\ge0}Z_{B,N}(J)z^N,\qquad \prod_{j\in J}(1+ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})=\sum_{N=0}^{|J|}Z_{F,N}(J)z^N.
$$
Each coefficient is the sum of the Boltzmann weights over the corresponding number sector; for a countable mode set it is the increasing limit over finite mode sets and is finite under the stated grand-trace hypotheses. A fixed-number law is the grand law conditioned on total number, so its occupations are generally coupled. The oscillator specialization uses the actual one-particle Hermite basis and diagonal domain of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], not a formal differential eigenfunction list.
